claims.text: Stable, coherent nanoscale precipitates in tungsten-based high-entropy alloys impede dislocation motion at high temperatures.
Such precipitates elevate high-temperature plastic strain by promoting dislocation accumulation and deflection.
Such precipitates elevate toughness by promoting crack-tip blunting.
A standard homogenization and aging treatment can produce coherent second-phase precipitates in the proposed tungsten-based high-entropy alloy ingots.
A dissolution heat treatment can significantly reduce the nanoscale precipitates while otherwise preserving a suitable comparison with precipitate-containing specimens.
Testing at or above 800 °C represents fusion-relevant service temperatures for the proposed material.
An inert testing environment prevents surface oxidation during the high-temperature mechanical tests.
Uniform coherent nanoprecipitates interact with both dislocations and crack tips in a tungsten-based high-entropy matrix.
Precipitates act as dislocation barriers or rerouting sites, increasing dislocation storage.
Increased dislocation storage and precipitate-mediated crack-tip shielding enhance both ductility and toughness at elevated temperature.
Precipitate-containing specimens will exhibit at least 10–20% greater plastic strain before fracture than precipitate-dissolved specimens.
Precipitate-containing specimens will exhibit greater fracture toughness than precipitate-dissolved specimens.
The mechanism should operate below the alloy's melting range and above its ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
Excessive precipitate coarsening, loss of coherence, or high-temperature instability may suppress the proposed mechanism.
The magnitude of the ductility and toughness changes depends on precipitate size, distribution, and alloy composition.
Side-by-side testing of otherwise identical precipitate-containing and precipitate-dissolved specimens is intended to isolate the precipitate contribution.
Comparable ductility and toughness in specimens with and without precipitates, or absence of a correlation with dislocation and crack-tip interactions, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention labels the precipitate-preserving group as the control, whereas the baseline field defines the precipitate-dissolved group as the baseline. The physical comparison is consistent, but the control/baseline terminology is inconsistent.
